nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; Victorian art criticism and political economy
literary_identity: Art critic, draughtsman, and social critic; the greatest English writer on art and the Victorian critic who turned from pictures to the political economy of labour.
biography: Born in London on 8 February 1819, the only child of a wealthy sherry merchant; educated privately and at Christ Church, Oxford, where he won the Newdigate prize in 1839. His mother moved with him to Oxford and read the Bible with him daily; his father financed the publication of Modern Painters I (1843), which defended Turner against the critics. He married Euphemia Gray in 1848; the marriage was annulled in 1854 after a famous and unhappy failure. The Stones of Venice (1851-53) established his reputation for architectural history, and from Unto This Last (1860, in the Cornhill) he turned to political economy and to the critique of Victorian capitalism. He was Slade Professor of Fine Art at Oxford from 1869 to 1879 and again in 1883-85, founded the Guild of St George (1871), published Fors Clavigera as letters to working men from 1871 to 1884, and suffered repeated mental breakdowns. He died at Brantwood, Coniston, on 20 January 1900.
literary_profile: Ruskin changed the way the Victorian age looked at art. His criticism begins with the truth to nature of the Pre-Raphaelites and Turner, passes to the moral and social analysis of architecture (the Stones of Venice's chapter 'The Nature of Gothic' makes the labour of the craftsman the test of art), and ends in a complete indictment of industrial capitalism as a system of slavery and ugliness. His prose is the most magnificent of Victorian descriptive writing — simple declarative sentences in the early work, and a wilder, evangelical, exclamatory manner in the late letters — and his method is always the accumulation of observed detail followed by a moral judgement that is both aesthetic and economic.
stylistic_characteristics: Precise, patient description of natural fact; the moral interpretation of ornament and building; direct address and personal confession; an apparently artless simplicity that carries a religious intensity; the letter form and the aphorism; the coined phrase ('the pathetic fallacy', 'the illth', 'There is no wealth but life').
intellectual_concerns: Truth to nature and the moral meaning of art; the relation of the artist's society to the art he makes; labour, craft and the dignity of the hand; the political economy of wealth and 'illth'; education and the reading of pictures; the destruction of the landscape by industry and tourism; the preservation of the past; the education of the working man.
historical_significance: Ruskin is the central English art critic and the origin of the idea that a society can be judged by its buildings. 'The Nature of Gothic' taught Morris and the Arts and Crafts movement that art was labour; Unto This Last gave the Labour movement and the founders of the British welfare state (Attlee and the Webbs) their moral vocabulary; the Pre-Raphaelites took their programme from him, and Pater, Wilde and the Aesthetic movement defined themselves by turning his moral criticism into an aesthetic one.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Poems (privately printed 1835); The Poetry of Architecture (1837-38); Modern Painters I (1843); II (1846); III (1856); IV (1856); V (1860); The Seven Lamps of Architecture (1849); The Stones of Venice (3 vols, 1851-53); Notes on the Construction of Sheepfolds (1851); Lectures on Architecture and Painting (1854); The Elements of Drawing (1857); Political Economy of Art (1857); The Two Paths (1859); Unto This Last (Cornhill 1860; book 1862); Munera Pulveris (1862-63); Sesame and Lilies (1865); The Ethics of the Dust (1866); The Crown of Wild Olive (1866); Time and Tide (1867); The Queen of the Air (1869); Lectures on Art (1870); Fors Clavigera: Letters to the Workmen and Labourers of Great Britain (8 vols, 1871-84); Munera Pulveris (1872); Ariadne Florentina (1872-76); Mornings in Florence (1875-77); Proserpina (1875-86); Deucalion (1875-83); St Mark's Rest (1877-84); The Laws of Fesole (1877-79); Fiction, Fair and Foul (1880); The Bible of Amiens (1880-85); The Storm-Cloud of the Nineteenth Century (1884); Praeterita (1885-89, unfinished autobiography); Hortus Inclusus (1887); The Art of England (1883).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; Victorian philosophy, political economy and political thought
literary_identity: Philosopher, political economist, civil servant and feminist; the central liberal thinker of the nineteenth century.
biography: Born in London on 20 May 1806, the eldest son of the Scottish philosopher James Mill, who educated him from the age of three with the rigour recorded in the Autobiography (1873): he read Greek at three, had mastered the whole of political economy by thirteen, and suffered a crisis at twenty from which he was saved by Wordsworth's poetry and by the love of Harriet Taylor, whom he married in 1851 after twenty years of attachment. He worked for the East India Company from 1823 to 1858, was elected to Parliament for Westminster in 1865, and moved the amendment that gave women the vote in 1867, defeating his own party. His books include the System of Logic (1843), Principles of Political Economy (1848), On Liberty (1859), Considerations on Representative Government (1861), Utilitarianism (1863), An Examination of Sir William Hamilton's Philosophy (1865) and The Subjection of Women (1869). He died at Avignon on 8 May 1873.
literary_profile: Mill refashioned Bentham's and his father's utilitarianism into a philosophy capable of defending individuality and liberty. His System of Logic established the methods of empirical science as the model of reasoning, and On Liberty set out the harm principle — the only ground for restricting a person's liberty is to prevent harm to others — which became the foundation of modern liberal thought. In political economy he distinguished the laws of production from the possible distribution of wealth, opening the way for a socialist and reformist economics; in The Subjection of Women he produced the most rigorous philosophical argument for women's equality in the nineteenth century.
stylistic_characteristics: Lucid, measured, and famously qualified prose; the argument by distinction and by the counter-example; the use of a stated 'exception' to define a rule; the conversion of philosophical positions into historical narratives of their development; personal confession used as evidence (the Autobiography).
intellectual_concerns: Liberty of thought and expression; individuality and the tyranny of opinion; the subjection of women; the aim of utilitarian ethics and the quality of pleasures; representative government and the democratic danger of mediocrity; the logic of induction; the economics of distribution and the 'stationary state'.
historical_significance: Mill is the father of modern liberalism and the most rigorous exponent of the Victorian liberal mind: On Liberty, Utilitarianism, and The Subjection of Women are foundational documents of modern politics, and his amendment on women's suffrage began the parliamentary campaign that ended in 1918 and 1928. His System of Logic shaped the social sciences, and his Principles of Political Economy taught the century economics until Marshall superseded it.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: The Spirit of the Age (1831); Essays on Some Unsettled Questions of Political Economy (1844); A System of Logic, Ratiocinative and Inductive (1843); Principles of Political Economy (1848); Thoughts on Parliamentary Reform (1859); On Liberty (1859); Dissertations and Discussions (4 vols, 1859-75); Considerations on Representative Government (1861); Utilitarianism (1863); An Examination of Sir William Hamilton's Philosophy (1865); Auguste Comte and Positivism (1865); The Subjection of Women (1869, with Harriet Taylor Mill); Chapters and Speeches on the Irish Land Question (1870); Autobiography (posthumous, 1873); Three Essays on Religion (posthumous, 1874); On Social Freedom (posthumous); Principles of Political Economy (People's Edition 1865).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; Victorian religious prose and the Oxford Movement
literary_identity: Clergyman, theologian, novelist, poet and cardinal; the leader of the Oxford Movement and the period's greatest religious autobiographer.
biography: Born in London on 21 February 1801, son of a banker; educated at Ealing and Trinity College, Oxford, where he became a fellow of Oriel in 1822 and vicar of St Mary's in 1828. His Evangelical conversion at fifteen and his subsequent High Church convictions made him the intellectual leader of the Oxford Movement from Keble's assize sermon of 1833; he edited the Tracts for the Times and was the author of Tract 90 (1841), which sought to reconcile the Thirty-Nine Articles with Catholic doctrine. The storm that followed drove him out of Oxford to Littlemore, where he was received into the Roman Catholic Church in October 1845. He founded the Oratory at Birmingham, was a moving and much-loved preacher, wrote the Apologia Pro Vita Sua in 1864 in answer to Charles Kingsley's charge of dishonesty, and was made a cardinal by Pope Leo XIII in 1879. He died at Edgbaston on 11 August 1890.
literary_profile: Newman's prose is the finest of all Victorian religious writing: measured, cadenced, exact, and utterly without Carlyle's prophetic violence. His subject is the grounds of belief — conscience, probability, the convergence of independent evidence, the 'illative sense' — and his method is the autobiographical narrative that turns the history of a mind into an argument. The Apologia is the great Victorian spiritual autobiography and a masterpiece of self-defence; the sermons and the lectures on the Idea of a University are the foundation of modern thinking about the purpose of liberal education; the poem The Dream of Gerontius became, in Elgar's setting, a central work of the English musical and religious tradition.
stylistic_characteristics: Ciceronian periods built on antithesis and climax; a personal voice of great courtesy and precision; the careful accumulation of probability rather than the assertion of certainty; theological vocabulary handled with legal exactness; the use of letters and documents as the substance of argument.
intellectual_concerns: The authority of conscience; faith and the cumulative argument; development in doctrine; the relation of the university to the Church and to knowledge; the claims of Rome against the Church of England; death, judgment and the soul's journey; the education of the gentleman.
historical_significance: Newman is the intellectual centre of the Oxford Movement and one of the greatest of English prose writers: the Apologia created the modern religious autobiography, the Idea of a University defined the modern debate about liberal education, and Gerontius gave the English oratorio its greatest subject. His theory of the 'development' of doctrine changed Catholic theology, and his account of the illative sense is a permanent contribution to the theory of knowledge.
biographical_uncertainty: Newman's Anglican and Catholic sources and his use of his own letters in the Apologia have been scrutinised since Kingsley's attack of 1864; the standard scholarly account is Ian Ker's biography (1988) and the Oxford Authors edition of the Apologia.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; Victorian religious poetry and the Oxford Movement
literary_identity: Poet, clergyman and professor; the devotional poet whose Christian Year was the most widely read poetry book of the Victorian age, and by tradition the first mover of the Oxford Movement.
biography: Born at Fairford on 25 April 1792, son of a clergyman; educated at Corpus Christi College, Oxford, where he became a fellow in 1811 and won the Newdigate prize. The Christian Year, published anonymously in 1827, sold by the thousand and remained in print throughout the century. His assize sermon on 'National Apostasy' at Oxford in July 1833 is conventionally taken as the beginning of the Oxford Movement; he contributed Tracts for the Times and his life of Bishop Wilson. He was Professor of Poetry at Oxford (1831-41), and in 1836 became vicar of Hursley, Hampshire, where he lived in obscurity until his death on 29 March 1866, cared for by his wife Charlotte and his sister Anne.
literary_profile: The Christian Year is a cycle of poems for every Sunday and holy day of the Book of Common Prayer, designed as family devotion: each poem takes the Gospel and Epistle of the day and turns them into a meditative lyric of nature, remembered childhood and moral reflection. Keble's verse is plain and its music is unostentatious; its power is the power of the Prayer Book, and it gave the Tractarian movement its devotional idiom. His prose (the sermons, the Life of Bishop Wilson) is practical and unadorned. His most influential criticism is the Latin lecture on the 'primitive' and the modest claim that poetry is the indirect expression of wishes for what we cannot attain.
stylistic_characteristics: Simple, traditional metre and a limited imagery of nature and childhood; the structure of the liturgical year; the refraining phrase and the mild warning; the absence of any but the most conventional poetic ornament; the sustaining of a single tone of trusting sentiment through 109 poems.
intellectual_concerns: The Church, the sacraments and the liturgical year; nature as a sign of grace; childhood and death; providence and resignation; the beauty of holiness and the danger of reform.
historical_significance: The Christian Year was the most influential book of devotional poetry in nineteenth-century England and shaped the spirituality of the Oxford Movement; Keble's assize sermon is the formal opening of the Tractarian controversy, and his influence on Newman, Pusey and the devotional verse of Christina Rossetti is direct. Its later neglect is itself a document of the Victorian crisis of faith it so thoroughly ignored.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: The Christian Year (1827, anonymous); Lyra Apostolica (contributor, 1836); Tract 4, Tract 10, Tract 52, Tract 89 (Tracts for the Times); The Life of Bishop Wilson (1863); Sermons Academical and Occasional (1847); Sermons for the Christian Year (posthumous, 11 vols, 1875-80); De Poeticae Vi Medica (Latin lectures, Oxford, 1844); On Eucharistical Adoration (1857); Letters of Spiritual Counsel (posthumous).

literary_identity: Poet and translator; the author of the Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám and the greatest English translator of Persian verse.
biography: Born at Bredfield on 31 March 1809 into an old Suffolk family of Irish descent; educated at Bury St Edmunds and Trinity College, Cambridge, where he met Thackeray and, through him, Tennyson, whose friend and correspondent he remained. He published Euphranor (1851), a dialogue on education, and Polonius (1852), a collection of aphorisms; he learned Spanish and translated Calderón, and in 1859 published the Rubáiyát anonymously in a paper wrapper, priced at one shilling. It was ignored until Rossetti and his circle found it in 1861; FitzGerald then revised it, and the fourth edition of 1879 made it famous. He translated the Agamemnon of Aeschylus (1865) and the Oedipus Tyrannus (1881) and lived the life of a solitary country reader and sailor, dying at Merton, Norfolk, on 14 June 1883.
literary_profile: The Rubáiyát is a free translation and rearrangement of the Persian quatrains of Omar Khayyám into English stanzas; FitzGerald made it a poem of Victorian melancholy — the potter, the sultan, the veiled figure, the wine, the 'Book of Verses underneath the Bough' — in which the pleasures of the present are the answer to a world without a future. His verse is quiet, exact and resigned, and his translations from the Greek are among the boldest and most successful of the century in rendering the feel of the original. The letters are the finest in Victorian English after those of Keats and Lamb.
stylistic_characteristics: The Rubáiyát stanza (aaba, adapted from the Persian quatrain); a plain syntax and a complete absence of ornament; the personification of the potter, the pot and the cup; the refrain and the variation; a tone of amused resignation.
intellectual_concerns: The uncertainty of life and the brevity of pleasure; the mystery of creation and the futility of speculation; the potter and the clay as emblems of the soul; death, dust and resurrection; wine, love and the 'paradise enow' of the present.
historical_significance: The Rubáiyát is the most popular English poem of the later nineteenth century and the origin of the vogue for Persian literature in English; its philosophy of 'a jug of wine, a loaf of bread' shaped the aesthetic and the melancholy of the 1890s, and its stanzas were among the most quoted lines in the English-speaking world. FitzGerald's translations of Aeschylus are still read, and his letters are a permanent record of the Victorian circle of Tennyson and Thackeray.
biographical_uncertainty: The Rubáiyát is a creative adaptation rather than a literal translation: FitzGerald reversed the order of the quatrains, invented some stanzas, and built a continuous poem out of material scattered in Omar's Persian. The fifth edition (1889) is the text usually reprinted.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; Victorian political science, economics and criticism
literary_identity: Economist, political journalist and critic; the founder of the modern study of the English constitution and one of the finest Victorian essayists.
biography: Born at Langport on 3 February 1826, son of a Unitarian banker; educated at Bristol and University College London, where he took a degree in mathematics. He read for the bar, joined his father's bank, and in 1857 became a partner and married Eliza Wilson, daughter of the founder of the Economist; from 1861 to his death he was the editor of the Economist, shaping it into the leading journal of liberal economics. The English Constitution (1867) is his masterpiece; Physics and Politics (1872) applied the new ideas of evolution to the development of nations, and Lombard Street (1873) is a classic account of the money market. He published Literary Studies (1879) and Economic Studies (1880) posthumously and died of pneumonia at Langport on 24 March 1877.
literary_profile: Bagehot's method is the description of an institution as it actually works rather than as it is described by its official theory. The English Constitution distinguishes the 'dignified' from the 'efficient' parts of the constitution — the monarchy and the Lords as the symbols that make the system acceptable, the cabinet as the real executive — and that distinction became the essential tool of political science. His style is the best of Victorian journalism: concrete, epigrammatic, faintly mocking, and capable of large generalisations resting on a single vivid case. He is also an acute literary critic who wrote on Shakespeare, Arnold, Tennyson and the Victorian novel.
stylistic_characteristics: Epigram and paradox; the concrete example used to test a large proposition; the distinction of the nominal from the real; the ironic understatement; a domesticate vocabulary for technical subjects; the long essay as the vehicle of ideas.
intellectual_concerns: The working of representative government; the relation of the Crown, the Lords and the Commons; the psychology of a free people and of an hereditary monarchy; evolution and social progress; the money market and the crises of credit; character and literature.
historical_significance: The English Constitution is the founding work of modern political science in Britain, and its distinction between the 'dignified' and 'efficient' constitution is still the standard analysis of the British system. Lombard Street is the origin of the modern theory of central banking and the lender of last resort, and Physics and Politics introduced evolutionary theory into the study of nations.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; Victorian satire, fiction and Darwinian controversy
literary_identity: Novelist, satirist, translator and controversialist; the most anti-Victorian of the Victorians, and the author of Erewhon and The Way of All Flesh.
biography: Born at Bingham on 4 December 1835, son of a clergyman and grandson of the headmaster of Shrewsbury; he was educated at Shrewsbury under his grandfather and at St John's College, Cambridge, and ran away to Canterbury, New Zealand, in 1859 rather than take orders, where he made money as a sheep farmer. He returned to London in 1864 and became a painter, musician and writer. Erewhon appeared anonymously in 1872, The Fair Haven in 1873, Life and Habit in 1877, Evolution Old and New in 1879, Unconscious Memory in 1880 and his prose translations of the Iliad (1898) and Odyssey (1900). The Way of All Flesh was written in 1873-84 and published posthumously in 1903; he died in London on 18 June 1902, leaving his money to found a controversy on the authorship of the Odyssey.
literary_profile: Butler wrote against the grain of Victorian belief: against the literalism of the Christian creed, against the Darwinism of Darwin himself (he argued for the inherited memory of habit and attacked the mechanism of natural selection), against the family, the school, and the cult of money. Erewhon is a Swiftian imaginary country whose institutions invert English ones — criminals are treated as invalids, illness is punished — and whose 'Book of the Machines' is the first serious English account of the possibility of machine consciousness. The Way of All Flesh is a satirical family chronicle of four generations of clergymen, and it became one of the defining attacks on Victorian patriarchy.
stylistic_characteristics: Swiftian inversion and the invented institution; a plain, sceptical, argumentative prose in the essays; in the fiction, the ironic narrator and the family chronicle; the use of the imaginary society to test the real one; epigram and the deliberately flat conclusion.
intellectual_concerns: The mechanical and the purposive in evolution; the machine and its possible consciousness; the tyranny of the Victorian family and the clergy; hypocrisy, money and respectability; the authorship of the Odyssey; religion as a provisional hypothesis.
historical_significance: Butler is the great anti-Victorian satirist and the direct ancestor of the twentieth-century 'strangers to the Victorian age': The Way of All Flesh was a central influence on Butler's admirers, on Shaw, and on Samuel Butler studies at the beginning of modern English literature; Erewhon's Book of the Machines is a foundational text of the literature of artificial intelligence, and his Homeric translations remain among the most readable in English.
bibliographical_notes: Other documented writings, recorded here because no separate work record with a verifiable description can be supported: Erewhon: or, Over the Range (1872, anonymous); The Fair Haven (1873, as 'William B. Owen'); Life and Habit (1877); Evolution Old and New (1879); Unconscious Memory (1880); Alps and Sanctuaries (1881); Luck, or Cunning? (1887); Ex Voto (1888); The Life and Letters of Dr Samuel Butler (his grandfather, 1896); The Authoress of the Odyssey (1897); Note-Books (posthumous, 1912); The Way of All Flesh (posthumous, 1903); Erewhon Revisited (1901); Selected Essays (1927).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; Victorian feminism, political economy and social thought
literary_identity: Philosopher and essayist; the intellectual partner of John Stuart Mill and a founding thinker of Victorian liberal feminism.
biography: Born Harriet Hardy in London in October 1807 and married at eighteen to the wholesale druggist John Taylor, by whom she had three children. Her friendship with John Stuart Mill began in 1830, and the scandal of their attachment — she separated from Taylor but remained married to him until his death in 1849 — caused her exclusion from respectable society. She married Mill in April 1851. Between 1848 and 1858 she wrote a series of essays, chiefly on the position of women and on the moral character of the age; the most substantial is The Enfranchisement of Women (1851), published anonymously in the Westminster Review. She died of consumption at Avignon in November 1858, and Mill lived afterwards at Avignon to be near her grave.
literary_profile: Harriet Taylor Mill's writings are few and difficult to disentangle from Mill's: The Enfranchisement of Women argued for women's suffrage and for their admission to all the professions at a time when the public campaign had barely begun, and her essays on toleration and on the moral 'improvement' of society anticipate the argument of On Liberty. Mill states in the Autobiography that her influence was decisive for On Liberty and for The Subjection of Women, and recent scholarship has established her as an independent thinker rather than a mere collaborator.
stylistic_characteristics: Polemical clarity and a command of the vocabulary of rights; the argument from the perversion of women's nature by constraint; an emphasis on the moral and intellectual benefits of equality to men; the use of concrete examples of the legal disabilities of married women.
intellectual_concerns: The legal and educational subordination of women; the moral consequences of the double standard; toleration and the limits of social opinion; the relation of personal freedom to social progress; the use of 'nature' as an instrument of custom.
historical_significance: Harriet Taylor Mill is a founding figure of the liberal feminist tradition and the intellectual origin of the two greatest works of Victorian feminism: On Liberty and The Subjection of Women. The Enfranchisement of Women is the first sustained English argument for women's suffrage, and her recovery in the later twentieth century (the Hayek edition of the Mill–Taylor correspondence, and the modern biographies) has changed the history of English political thought.
biographical_uncertainty: Her authorship and her influence on Mill have been much disputed since the nineteenth century. The attribution of The Enfranchisement of Women is established by Mill's papers and by the Westminster Review's records; the extent of her share in On Liberty and The Subjection of Women is argued by Hayek, Rossi and Jacobs, and the honest position is that the exact division of labour cannot be documented.
